title: The Man Who Wanted to be God (简体中文)
summary: An arrogant ascetic claims he has attained divine godhood and demands worship. Birbal tests his claim with a task only God can perform. [ZH]
keywords: the man who wanted to be god
full_text:
A strange, haughty mendicant dressed in saffron silk arrived in Agra, followed by dozens of gullible disciples. The man proclaimed himself an incarnation of the Supreme Divine, shouting in the public square:

'I have conquered the elements! I am God walking upon earth! All emperors, kings, and mortals must prostrate before me and offer their wealth, or be burned by my divine wrath!'

Brought before Emperor Akbar, the arrogant ascetic refused to bow, sneering: 'Why should God bow to a mortal king? Emperor, surrender your throne, for I am the ruler of the universe!'

Akbar was annoyed, but hesitated to punish a man claiming spiritual authority. He looked to Birbal for counsel.

Birbal stepped forward, bowed politely to the ascetic, and said:

'O Holy Divinity! If you are indeed the Supreme Creator of the universe, our court rejoices! For we have an urgent problem that only God Himself can solve.'

The ascetic puffed up with pride: 'Speak! There is nothing impossible for my divine will!'

Birbal said: 'Our imperial treasury is vast, yet our people often suffer from drought. Since you are the Creator, we request that you perform one simple divine miracle before this assembly right now:

'Create one single, living honeybee out of nothingness—not out of clay, not out of wax, but breath and soul—and make it fly across this room, sip nectar, and live!'

The ascetic stammered: 'That is a minor trick! God does not perform parlor magic!'

'Very well,' Birbal continued with razor sharpness. 'Then perform the second attribute of the Divine:

'A king must punish criminals with the sword, for he is only human. But God is the All-Forgiving, who forgives the sins of millions without demanding a single copper coin.

'Therefore, forgive this courtier who is about to spit upon your robe, and forgive the guards who are about to take your golden ornaments and distribute them to the starving orphans of Agra—and show us your divine love by blessing them with joy!'

The ascetic turned pale as milk. He clutched his silk robes, backed away from the guards, and began to tremble.

Birbal looked at the Emperor: 'Sire, this man has the pride of a demon, but neither the power of creation nor the mercy of forgiveness. He is an ordinary fraud who seeks worship to fill his pockets.'

Humbled and terrified, the charlatan fell to his knees, admitted his deception, and begged for mercy. Akbar banished him from Agra, praising Birbal for defending true spiritual dignity.
